dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The report reinforces the cluster’s operating-model thesis with multinational survey evidence that legal departments are responding to rising demand through process redesign, heavier technology use and AI investment. It materially extends the synthesis by documenting the legal-operations structures, repeatable processes, governance and stable technology associated with organisational maturity, while not establishing AI capability, verification quality or realised productivity gains.

st.t: Legal departments: AI supports selective sourcing redesign
st.an: CLOC supports the cluster’s nuanced account: rising demand is prompting departments to combine greater use of existing teams, technology, process redesign and AI, while current AI deployment remains materially below planned adoption. Its respondent-reported benchmarks describe operating-model and provider-management changes, not proven productivity gains, uniform budget contraction or wholesale substitution of outside counsel.

kp.k: Survey benchmarks corporate legal operations across 186 organizations
kp.d: The report draws on the 2024 Harbor Law Department Survey in collaboration with CLOC, covering 186 organizations across more than 15 industries and 14 countries. Its findings concern participating corporate legal departments, including spending, staffing, technology and outside counsel management.
qs: Based on the 2024 Harbor Law Department Survey in Collaboration with CLOC, this report captures benchmarks from 186 diverse organizations.
The survey contained responses from 186 organizations across more than 15 industries and 14 countries.

kp.k: AI adoption increases, with further implementation under consideration
kp.d: The quick statistics section reports AI implementation and use at 30%, up from 18% in 2023, and consideration of implementation within one to two years at 54%, up from 40% the previous year. The technology chart instead reports 29% AI use and lists a homegrown solution as the most-used provider. The priorities section describes the 54% as planning implementation rather than merely considering it; these prospective responses are distinct from deployed use.
qs: The adoption of AI has increased significantly
Emerging technologies are also a focus, with Artificial Intelligence seeing a significant increase in consideration for future implementation in this year's survey.
This emphasis aligns with the increasing adoption of artificial intelligence and workflow tools, as 54% plan to implement AI and 33% plan to adopt workflow tools within the next one to two years.

kp.k: Growing demand pressures existing teams and resources
kp.d: The narrative reports that 83% of departments expect legal demand to grow, whereas the accompanying graphic reports 80%. Workload and resource bandwidth are identified as the top challenge by 63%. Reported responses include increasing existing teams' workload (39%), greater use of current technology (36%), process re-engineering or standardization (36%), and AI investment (21%). These are reported strategies, not evidence of achieved productivity gains.
qs: 83% of departments expect demand for legal services to continue growing, with 63% identifying workload and resource bandwidth as their top challenge.

To handle the increase in volume of legal work, law departments are pursuing a range of strategies: increasing the workload of existing legal teams (39%); increasing their use of current technology (36%); re-engineering and/or standardizing work processes (36%); and investing in AI (21%).

kp.k: Automation and technology remain leading departmental priorities
kp.d: In the priorities-for-2025 section, 66% identify legal-process automation as a high priority. The chart also identifies implementing a new technology solution as a high priority for 62% and rightsourcing legal work between in-house teams and outside counsel for 49%. The report describes automation and technology implementation as persistent priorities since 2020, rather than a wholly new response to AI.
qs: Legal departments continue to prioritize automation, with 66% of respondents identifying it as a high priority.
Since 2020, automation and new technology implementation have remained top concerns, with more than half of respondents ranking them as key focus areas.

kp.k: Established legal technologies remain more widespread than AI
kp.d: The technology chart reports electronic billing use at 84%, document management and matter management at 72% each, legal hold at 71%, and contract lifecycle management at 62%. Workflow automation is used by 44% and legal service request/intake tools by 37%, compared with AI at 29% in this chart. These figures describe technology use, not demonstrated task substitution or reductions in staffing.
qs: The most widely used technology areas in participating legal departments include eBilling, Document Management, and Matter Management.

kp.k: ALSP work remains limited but service scope expands
kp.d: The report allocates 60% of work to in-house legal teams, 35% to outside counsel and 5% to other service providers/ALSPs. It describes growing ALSP adoption for cost efficiency, extending beyond e-discovery to attorney contractors, staff augmentation and contract management. The leading reported uses are e-discovery processing and hosting (58%), attorney contractors/staff augmentation (52%), and e-discovery document review (49%). The report does not attribute this expansion specifically to AI.
qs: Law departments across industries are increasingly turning to non-law firm resources to improve cost efficiency.
While spending on alternative legal service providers (ALSPs) remains a small portion of total legal spend, adoption is growing.
Historically used primarily for e-Discovery, ALSPs are now being leveraged more for attorney contractors, staff augmentation, and contract management.

kp.k: Legal spending rises with respondent-mix qualifications
kp.d: Reported median internal expenditure is $21.7 million and external expenditure $20.6 million, compared with $20.1 million and $19.5 million respectively in 2023. The report attributes part of the increase to changes in participating companies. Its company-size table reports overall medians of $49.7 million total legal spend, $1.4 million ALSP spend and $701.9K legal systems and technology spend. External spend is defined as outside counsel spend only.
qs: This increase in median spending is, in part, due to the shift in the mix of participating companies.
Note: Median values reported for all metrics.
includes outside counsel spend

kp.k: Company size shapes internal versus external spending
kp.d: The expenditure-balance figures report internal spending at 45% and external spending at 49% overall. Companies below $3 billion revenue report 58% internal and 38% external, while companies above $40 billion report 41% internal and 54% external. The report presents company size as a factor in resource allocation; it does not establish that AI caused these differences.
qs: Company size plays a role, with smaller companies (under $3 billion in revenue) spending significantly more in-house, while larger companies allocate more to external expenditures.

kp.k: Department staffing scales with company size
kp.d: Median legal department staffing is 77 FTEs overall, increasing from 13 in companies below $3 billion revenue to 244 above $40 billion. Median attorney headcount is 44 overall. The report states that smaller companies have more other legal professionals per attorney; these are departmental staffing benchmarks, not law-firm leverage measures or evidence of AI displacement.
qs: The median legal department headcount is 77 Full - Time Employees (FTEs) across all participating companies, with staff size increasing alongside company size.
When examining department headcount by company size, the median attorney headcount is 44 across all participating companies, with staff size increasing alongside company size.
Smaller companies have a higher proportion of other legal professionals, such as support and operations staff, per attorney in their department.

kp.k: Legal operations staffing remains stable despite broader demands
kp.d: The legal operations section reports an unchanged median team size of five FTEs since 2023. It gives company-size medians of 2, 4, 7 and 10 FTEs, while the preceding headcount table lists 2, 3, 6 and 8 legal operations professionals for the same revenue bands. The document does not explain this difference. It reports the highest revenue-normalized operations staffing in technology departments, at 0.39 staff per $1 billion revenue.
qs: The size of legal operations teams has remained unchanged since 2023, with a median function size of 5 FTEs.
Technology departments report the highest staffing levels, with 0.39 legal operations staff per $1B in revenue.

kp.k: Legal operations manages technology, vendors and service delivery
kp.d: At least half of departments assign 12 of the 15 listed services to legal operations. The most common responsibilities are outside counsel/vendor management (95%), technology strategy (91%), technology administration (88%), program/project management (84%) and financial management (80%). The report describes growth of 7% in business intelligence responsibilities and 5% in service delivery models since the previous year.
qs: At least 50% of departments have 12 of the 15 services listed below within their legal operations team’s responsibilities.
The top five most common services remain unchanged, but business intelligence and service delivery models have grown by 7% and 5%, respectively, since the previous year.

kp.k: Operations leadership is usually formalized and full-time
kp.d: The report states that more than half of participants have a team with formal operations responsibilities reporting to a director or manager. Its charts show 87% of leadership roles are full-time, with 56% reporting to the CLO/GC and 32% to an AGC/DGC. These findings describe the organization of the corporate buyer-side function.
qs: More than 50% of participants report having a team with formal legal operations responsibilities reporting to a Director or Manager of Legal Operations.
This role is typically full-time and reports directly to the CLO or GC.

kp.k: Outside counsel selection emphasizes individual expertise
kp.d: The report states that 38% have implemented or are refining structured annual firm performance evaluations and another 17% plan formal reviews. For outside counsel selection, 87% rate a particular lawyer's expertise as very important, compared with 59% for knowledge of the organization and 39% for firm market reputation. These are firm evaluation and purchasing criteria, not verification of AI output.

kp.k: Self-reported operational maturity varies with company size
kp.d: Most respondents identify their departments as emerging to developing. The developing-to-leading category accounts for 8% of companies below $3 billion revenue, 27% at $3B–$15B, 33% at $15B–$40B and 43% above $40 billion. These are reported maturity classifications, not measured AI capability or proof that technology adoption produces organizational maturity.
qs: Most identify as emerging to developing, indicating room for growth.
As resources expand and best practices evolve, maturity levels continue to advance, driving greater optimization and efficiency.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: CLOC and Harbor report increased AI adoption and prospective implementation in corporate legal departments, with AI investment among their responses to growing workloads.
pts.d: The report's quick statistics state that 30% have an AI tool implemented and in use, compared with 18% in 2023, and that 54% are considering implementation within one to two years, compared with 40% previously. The technology chart separately reports AI use at 29% and identifies a homegrown solution as the most-used provider category. The priorities section describes the 54% as planning, rather than considering, implementation. The report also states that 21% are investing in AI to handle increased legal work. These are adoption and strategy claims, not findings that AI has already reduced costs, improved output or displaced staff. Automation and new-technology priorities are broader than AI alone.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims are based on respondent-reported adoption, intentions and priorities in the 2024 Harbor Law Department Survey in collaboration with CLOC.
pts.d: The 2025 report describes a sample of 186 organizations across more than 15 industries and 14 countries. Its evidence consists of survey benchmarks and comparisons with previous survey results. The supplied report does not provide AI performance tests, measured productivity gains, causal estimates or AI-specific staffing outcomes. It does not specify item-level response counts or whether the same organizations underpin the year-to-year AI comparison.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current adoption reflects the 2024 survey, compared with 2023; prospective AI implementation concerns the following one to two years.
pts.d: Although published as a 2025 report, the findings derive from the 2024 survey. The one-to-two-year implementation horizon is a reported intention or consideration, not a confirmed deployment outcome. The priorities section is headed 'PRIORITIES FOR 2025' and links these intentions to a continuing emphasis on automation and new technology since 2020. AI investment is presented specifically as one strategy for handling increased work volume.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are corporate legal departments and the legal operations professionals responsible for technology and workload management.
pts.d: The source addresses the buyer side of legal services: in-house legal teams managing increased demand and legal operations teams overseeing technology strategy and administration. AI is presented as part of their operational response, alongside existing technology, process redesign and greater workloads for current staff. The report does not attribute changes in law-firm employment, ALSP market share or public access to justice to AI.
